title: Find All Anagrams in a String — fixed-size window with frequency comparison.
shortTitle: Find All Anagrams in a String — Fixed-Size Window With Frequency Comparison

s1_definition.profdef: This problem returns the start indexes of every substring of a text that is an anagram of a given pattern. A fixed-size sliding window the length of the pattern slides across the text, maintaining a character-frequency count that is compared against the pattern's frequency; a match means the window is an anagram. Using a matched-count optimization it runs in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks for every place in a transaction-reference string where a window of characters is a rearrangement of a known suspicious code. Rajesh slides a fixed-width window the size of the code and keeps a tally of letters inside it; whenever the tally matches the code's tally, that starting spot is an anagram hit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window the size of the pattern and compare character counts; equal counts mean the window is an anagram.

sections.s3_flow:
```
  text="cbaebabacd" pattern="abc"
    │
    ▼
  slide width-3 window; compare window freq to need freq
    │ window[0..2]="cba" == need → start 0
    │ window[1..3]="bae" ≠
    │ ...
    │ window[6..8]="bac" == need → start 6
    ▼
  Result: [0, 6]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Find All Anagrams in a String returns the starting index of every window in a text that is a rearrangement of a given pattern, and I solve it with a fixed-size sliding window the length of the pattern. I build a character-frequency count for the pattern, then slide a same-width window across the text, adding the character entering on the right and removing the character leaving on the left. Whenever the window reaches the pattern's width, I compare the window's frequency count against the pattern's; if they are equal the window is an anagram and I record its starting index.

There are two ways to do the comparison. The straightforward way compares the two frequency arrays at each position, which costs a constant factor of twenty-six per step and is still linear in the length of the text. The faster way maintains a single matched-letter counter that updates incrementally as characters enter and leave, reporting a hit when all twenty-six letters match, which removes that constant factor. Both are acceptable, and I usually reach for the array comparison first because it is easier to get right under pressure and mention the matched-count optimization as the improvement.

The details that catch people out are the off-by-one on when to start comparing, which is only once the window has grown to the full pattern width, and remembering to drop the character that slides off the left edge as the window advances, otherwise the counts drift and every later comparison is wrong.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud service. The team had a known suspicious character pattern and needed every position in a long transaction-reference string where a same-length window was a permutation of it, since fraud rings sometimes reorder a code. The reference strings were long, so the linear sliding comparison was essential rather than checking each substring independently. Explaining the window slide, the frequency comparison, the matched-count optimization, and the off-by-one and shrink details shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and the pitfalls.

Remember one sentence: understand the core algorithm and apply it to banking domain problems.

keyPoints: String manipulation: reverse, palindrome, anagram check
String is immutable in Java — use StringBuilder for modification
Build a frequency array `need` of size 26 for the pattern.
Slide a window of width equal to the pattern length over the text, keeping a `window` frequency array.
For each new right index add its character to `window`, and once the window exceeds the pattern length, remove the leftmost character.
